verdict: Same five colours, same paper, same ink — B just can't tell a noun from a verb. It paints 'spot' red inside 'helps you spot weak verbs' while colouring every other bare infinitive on the page blue, then drops 'repetitions' and 'clutter' into body ink entirely and calls 'Check' a verb. states.name: all-dark
states.gap: Four words carry the wrong Category ink: 'repetitions' and 'clutter' are left in body grey #CCCCCC instead of noun red #CE896D; 'spot' — a verb in 'helps you spot weak verbs' — is painted noun red #CE896D where A gives it verb blue #829EBF; and in the proper noun 'Style Check', 'Style' is red but 'Check' is blue #829EBF, splitting one name across two Categories one line after B itself painted 'Syntax Highlight' red in full.
states.gapTheirs: Line pitch is not constant: baselines land at y=74/147/220/294, i.e. 73px, 73px, then 74px, so the fourth line sits 1px off the grid, where B holds a uniform 74px advance on all three gaps (x-height identical at 22px in both).
states.verdict: Both apps draw from the same five hexes — red CE896D, blue 829EBF, yellow B99558, green 89A474, purple B490B0 — so this is not a palette argument, it is a parsing argument, and B loses it. On the one line that matters B calls the verb 'spot' a noun and then fails to call the nouns 'repetitions' and 'clutter' anything at all, which is worse than no highlighting: a writer scanning for weak verbs is handed a red word that is a verb and a grey word that is a noun. B then breaks its own rule inside a line, painting 'Style' red and 'Check' blue after having painted 'Syntax Highlight' red end to end. A's only sin is a 1px stagger in the leading that nobody will notice; B's sins are the ones the feature exists to avoid.

states.name: focus-sentence
states.gap: Every Category carries less ink per word at the same viewport: 'Together' holds 1382 pure-#A6559F pixels inside a 205×41 box (16.4% coverage) against A's 1482 inside a 200×38 box (19.5%) — ~16% fainter per coloured word — and B runs the identical line 26px wider (right edge 1659 vs 1633), so the five hues are thinner and more spread across the measure.
states.gapTheirs: Caret renders #36BFFA — a lightened, greyed sky blue roughly 13% off the #00BFFF accent B lands exactly — and its 6×74px bar reaches full value on only 430 of 444 cells vs B's 444/444, so A's bar sits washed against the same ground (caret hue is the caret Piece's row, so this is the nearest measurable difference, not a syntax gap).
states.verdict: On the thing this piece actually decides, these two are the same page: all five Category hexes are byte-identical (#BB512A, #A6559F, #9D6722, #4675B5 on #F7F7F7, body #191919), the dimmed rows on both bottom out at exactly #C6C4C2 with zero saturated pixels above y=165, and both split it'll the same way — 'it' in body ink, apostrophe-and-'ll' in verb blue. So the choice comes down to how much of that colour survives onto the glyph, and A's is denser: a writer scanning for weak verbs picks the blue out of A's line faster than B's paler, wider setting. B's one visible tell — 'Check' painted verb-blue so the product name 'Style Check' fractures red/blue mid-phrase — is the shipped tagger's answer and I am not scoring it, but it is the kind of thing a writer will trip over and blame the colours for. Neither side has an actual gap here; A wins on colour weight and nothing else.
